 An EBT scam is any trick that gets your EBT card number or PIN, or your benefits, most often a text on your iPhone or Android phone saying your card is locked, or a skimmer on a store card reader. A real benefits office never asks for your PIN by text or phone: if you gave it out, change the PIN and call your state's EBT line today.
 By Ugnius Kiguolis Published October 25, 2026 10 min read 
 Facts checked October 25, 2026. Steps checked against Apple's and Google's current documentation and the reports we cite. We have not run the app or the link on a phone ourselves.
 Do it yourself · free Remove EBT scam yourself 6 steps, about 18 minutes, no software needed. 
 Start the steps ↓ How an EBT text scam usually runs, from the USDA and state attorney general warnings we read. EBT scam: summary
 Name EBT scam (EBT card text scam, SNAP skimming, fake benefits offers) 
 Type Phishing by text and phone, card skimming at store terminals, and fake offers about benefits; no single program or malware family 
 Risk High for the card holder: stolen benefits may not be replaced, and the money is often food money for a month 
 Symptoms A text or call saying the EBT card is locked or benefits will lapse; a balance lower than it should be; charges you did not make 
 How to get rid of it Nothing to uninstall. Stop replying, change the PIN, check the balance, tell your SNAP office, report the message 
 Our check (25 October 2026) No address to test: the subject is a name, not a website. We read USDA, FTC and state attorney general pages 
 Show 5 more facts Who can meet it Anyone who holds an EBT card in the United States, and anyone who receives a text about one 
 Microsoft detection None: this is fraud by message and by card reader, not a Windows threat 
 Evidence 0 write-ups by security sites; details still limited 
 First seen 25 October 2026 
 Facts checked 25 October 2026 
 Facts checked on 25 October 2026 against USDA's SNAP scam alerts page, the FTC consumer alert of May 2024, a New Hampshire attorney general notice of November 2025, news coverage of the end of federal replacement of stolen SNAP benefits and a New Jersey consumer alert. This subject is a name, not an address, so no request was made to any server. Some coverage is from 2025; state rules change.
 What people mean by an EBT scam
 "EBT scam" is not one scam. It is the name people use for several different tricks that all aim at the same thing: the Electronic Benefit Transfer card that holds food benefits (SNAP) and, in some states, cash benefits. Someone who searches for it has usually just received a text, a call or a social media message, or has found that money is missing from the card.
 The first kind is phishing. USDA's scam alerts page says criminals send fake texts claiming that a SNAP EBT card is locked, and the text includes a phone number to call.
 The person who answers asks for the card number and the PIN. USDA calls this a phishing scam and a form of fraud, and says plainly that you should not give your EBT card number or PIN by phone or text.
 The second kind is skimming. The Federal Trade Commission's consumer alert of May 2024 describes illegal skimmers placed on payment terminals in stores. A skimmer reads the magnetic stripe of the card.
 Because an EBT card needs a PIN, thieves may also put a hidden camera near the reader, or phish the PIN by text or call. With both, they make a duplicate card and drain the benefits.
 The third kind is the fake offer or fake help: a lookalike website or a caller who claims to be from the benefits office and says the card must be verified, unblocked or renewed.
 A New Jersey consumer alert on SNAP scams says that state agencies and SNAP workers will never ask for this kind of information over the phone or by text message, and that help with getting SNAP benefits is always free.
 This page covers all three, because the same reader meets all three. It is written for the person holding the card, and for the relative or caseworker who is helping them. It does not tell you that any named business or person is behind a scam: we found no primary source that does, and we say below what we could and could not confirm.
 What it targets The EBT card number, the PIN, and the benefits on the card Main routes Fake text about a locked card, phone call from a fake agent, skimmer on a store card reader, lookalike website What a real agency says USDA: do not give the card number or PIN by phone or text; ask your local SNAP office if unsure Nothing to install The harm comes from what you tell the sender, not from a file on your phone First move Stop replying, change the PIN, check the balance, tell the SNAP office The "your EBT card is locked" text
 A text that says your EBT card is locked, suspended or about to expire, and tells you to call a number or tap a link, is a scam until your own state's EBT customer service says otherwise. USDA's alert describes exactly this message, and the number in it leads to the people who want your PIN.
 The message works because it is short and urgent. It does not need to know your name. It is sent to very many phone numbers, and the senders count on a small share of recipients actually holding an EBT card. For those who do, the fear of losing the month's food money is strong, and the caller is practiced at keeping you on the line.
 Scam texts of this kind often claim that benefits are about to lapse and send you to a lookalike site where you are asked for the card number and PIN. A state benefits office does not work that way. Texts from a state can exist for real purposes, for example reminders, but a message that asks you to give the card number or the PIN is never one of them.
 A test you can run in a minute: ignore the number in the text and find your state's EBT customer service number yourself, from the back of your card or from your state's official benefits website. Call that number. If the card is fine, they will tell you. If the text was real, the real line can fix it without asking for your PIN in a text.
 What the text says What it wants What to do 
 Your EBT card is locked, call this number The card number and PIN, spoken on the phone Do not call. Call the number on the back of the card instead 
 Benefits will expire, tap to update your account Card number and PIN typed into a lookalike page Do not tap. Open your state's own site by typing its address 
 You qualify for extra benefits or a bonus A fee, or card details to receive it Ignore it. Real benefits are never sold and never need a fee 
 A caller says they are from the benefits office The PIN to verify you Hang up. Call your SNAP office on a number you looked up yourself 
 Dated warnings from the pages we read. They are separate notices, not one campaign. What the EBT scam message looks like
 The rule that never fails: a real agency does not ask for your PIN by text or phone, and does not need you to act within minutes. Everything else is a sign, not proof.
 Signs of a scam message
 Asks for the PIN
 Says the card is locked
 Gives a number to call
 Link in a text
 Urgent deadline
 Unknown sender
 Fee for help
 Promise of bonus benefits
 Asks to keep it secret
 Lookalike web address
 Do
 Look up your state's EBT customer service number yourself and call that. 
 Change your PIN now and then, and do not write it on the card. 
 Check the balance often, so a theft shows up the same day. 
 Look at the card reader before you swipe, for overlays or loose parts. 
 Ask your local SNAP office when you are unsure about a message. 
 Don't
 Give the card number or PIN to anyone who texts or calls you. 
 Tap a link in a text about your benefits. 
 Call the number that was in the message. 
 Pay anyone for help with SNAP, or for "recovering" stolen benefits. 
 Sell, lend or hand over the card. 
 How to tell the EBT scam message is fake
 You cannot stop the texts from arriving, but you can make them harmless and make theft show up fast.
 Keep the PIN in your head. Change it if anyone else has seen it. Check the balance after each shopping trip for the first weeks after a change of PIN, and at least weekly after that, because a skimmed card is usually emptied in a short time.
 Ask your state whether it offers a chip card, as USDA recommends, and whether it has a lock feature on the card or the app.
 If a relative or a caseworker helps with the card, agree on one rule: nobody gives the PIN to a third party. Tell older relatives about the locked card text in particular, because it is written to frighten people who live on a fixed income.
 On the phone itself, a message from an unknown number about benefits does not need an answer. Deleting it and blocking the sender is enough, and you do not have to open any link to do so.
 Is EBT scam dangerous? What the senders want
 Card skimming: how benefits disappear with no message at all
 With skimming you receive nothing and click nothing. A device on a store's card reader copies your card's magnetic stripe, and a camera or a phished PIN completes the theft. You find out when the balance is lower than it should be.
 The FTC alert explains that EBT cards need PINs, so scammers either phish the PIN with texts or calls or hide a camera near the skimmer. They then create duplicate cards and drain the benefits.
 USDA's guidance adds that thieves place a device on a retailer's card swiping machine, and it asks card holders to check readers for overlays that are bigger than the original machine or that hide parts of it.
 The magnetic stripe is the weak spot. A card that uses a chip is much harder to copy. USDA has recommended that states move SNAP and EBT to chip cards and described them as effective in protecting benefits from fraud.
 In spring 2025 news coverage, California and Oklahoma were reported to be working on the change, while Georgia said chip cards were not yet possible there because most EBT vendors' point of sale systems did not support them. That coverage is from 2025, so check what your state does now.
 You cannot remove a skimmer yourself, and you should not try to pull at a reader in a shop. Look before you swipe, tell the store staff if something looks odd, and use the reader that is built into the counter rather than a loose one if you have the choice.
 EBT scam · what we could and could not confirm · 25 October 2026
 Locked card text Described as an active phishing pattern on USDA's SNAP scam alerts page, with a phone number in the text. 
 Skimming Described in the FTC consumer alert of May 2024 and in USDA's guidance on card readers. 
 Phishing aimed at SNAP users A state attorney general in New Hampshire issued a warning in November 2025 and asked people to hang up on suspicious calls and report them. 
 Number of victims We found no reliable national count that we could confirm, so we give none. 
 Who runs the scams Not known. The sources we read do not name a group, and we do not name one. 
 A website or file to test None: the subject is a name, not an address, so no plain request was made. A quiet test would not clear anything anyway. 
 A real and current fraud pattern, with no single operator we can name The warnings come from USDA, the FTC and a state attorney general. Treat any message that asks for your card number or PIN as a scam.
 Will stolen EBT benefits be paid back?
 It depends on the date of the theft and on your state, and it is no longer guaranteed. Federal money for replacing stolen SNAP benefits covered thefts only until 20 December 2024.
 News coverage of the USDA notice says that benefits stolen on or after 21 December 2024 cannot be replaced with federal funds. Claims for thefts between 1 October 2022 and 20 December 2024 could still be sent to state agencies.
 States may choose to replace stolen benefits with their own money, but the coverage says there is no guarantee that this would be retroactive, and that many states had not planned for the cost.
 What this means for you:
 report the theft at once
 in writing if your state allows it
 ask your local SNAP office what your state does today
 Keep a note of the date, the amount, and the transactions you did not make. We could not confirm the current rules of each state, and they can change, so we do not list them. Your SNAP office is the only source that can tell you for your case.
 Fast reporting matters for another reason: the PIN and the card can be cancelled and replaced so that nothing more is taken. Every hour the old card stays active is an hour the thieves can spend what is left.
 The order of actions after EBT details were given to a scammer, following USDA and state advice. Fake help, fake offers and lookalike pages
 Any offer that puts a price on EBT help, or promises extra benefits, is a scam. Official help with SNAP is free, and no agency contacts recipients out of the blue to ask for private details.
 The state notices we read describe callers who pose as SNAP staff and ask for card details "to unblock the card" or "to verify eligibility". Other notices describe posts on social media that promise EBT deals or bonuses.
 These are hooks for your card number, your PIN and your personal data, and they appear more often when news about benefits is in the headlines. A New Jersey consumer alert was issued during the federal government shutdown for this reason.
 Selling or buying benefits is a different matter. State inspector general offices charge people who sell their benefits, sometimes through social media buy and sell pages.
 A reader who is offered cash for the card, or who is asked to hand over the card and PIN as a favor, risks losing the benefits and may also be breaking the rules of the program. We say this as a warning, not as legal advice.
 Do not trust a page because it looks official. Type your state's benefits address yourself, or use the one printed on letters you received by post, and do not tap addresses that arrive in texts.
 High Giving the PIN to a caller
 With the card number and PIN, a thief can spend the balance. A real agency does not need your PIN.
 High Typing details on a lookalike page
 The page may be a copy of a real site. The address is the only reliable sign: check it letter by letter.
 Medium Paying a fee for help
 Help with SNAP is free. A fee means the offer is not real.
 Medium Handing the card to a stranger
 A card handed over once can be copied or emptied, and selling benefits is treated as fraud.
 If you clicked the link or replied
 If you already gave your card number or PIN
 Act the same day. The goal is to make the old card number and PIN useless before the balance is spent. Nothing here needs special software, and none of it depends on which phone you use.
 1 Stop the contact
 Hang up, close the page, and do not reply to the text. Do not call back the number that was in the message. Keep the text itself, with its number and time, so you can report it.
 2 Change the PIN or cancel the card
 Call the customer service number printed on the back of your EBT card, the one you found on the card and not in the message. Ask to change the PIN, and if you gave the card number as well, ask for the card to be cancelled and replaced.
 3 Check the balance and the list of transactions
 Use the card's phone line or your state's official EBT site or app. Look for purchases you did not make. USDA's advice is to check the account for unauthorized charges and change the PIN right away if you find any.
 4 Tell your local SNAP office
 USDA says that if benefits were stolen you should contact your local SNAP office. Give the dates and amounts. Ask what your state does about replacement for thefts after 20 December 2024.
 5 Report the scam
 Report it to your state's attorney general or consumer protection office. In New Hampshire the attorney general's notice gives 1-844-ASK-DHHS for the benefits agency and 1-888-468-4454 for the Consumer Protection Bureau; in other states, look up your own state's offices.
 6 Watch for a second attempt
 People who answered once are often called again, for example by someone who offers to "recover" the stolen money for a fee. That is the same scam in a new form. Hang up.
 What we do not know
 We do not know who sends the locked card texts, how many people have lost money to them, or how each state handles replacement today. We say so because a guide that guessed would be worse than one that says it does not know.
 Our reading of the warnings is that skimming and phishing are linked: a skimmed card number is useful to a thief only with the PIN, and the texts and calls are one way to get it. The sources we read describe both together, but none of them proves that the same people do both.
 This page is not legal advice and it is not an official notice. For your case, the answers come from your state's benefits agency. The dates and rules above are those of the pages we read on 25 October 2026, and some of the news coverage is from 2025.
 What to do about an EBT scam text or call on iPhone and Android
 There is nothing to uninstall: the harm comes from what you told the sender.
 These steps work the same on an iPhone and on an Android phone.
 1 Step 1 : Stop and keep the message
 Warning: Do not reply, do not tap a link and do not call the number in the text.
 Keep the message on your iPhone or Android phone for now, because the number and the time help when you report it.
 If you tapped a link but typed nothing, nothing has been given away. If you typed the card number or PIN, go on at once.
 The order of actions after EBT details were given to a scammer. 
 2 Step 2 : Call the number on the back of the card
 Find the customer service number printed on your EBT card and call it from your phone. Do not use any number that came in a text. Ask to change the PIN.
 If you gave out the card number too, ask for the card to be cancelled and replaced, and write down the name or reference you are given.
 3 Step 3 : Check what has been spent
 Ask for the balance and the recent transactions on that call, or use your state's official EBT site or app by typing its address yourself.
 Look for purchases you do not recognize. USDA's advice is to change the PIN right away if you find unauthorized charges. Write down the dates and the amounts.
 4 Step 4 : Tell your local SNAP office
 Contact your local SNAP office, as USDA advises when benefits are stolen. Give the dates and amounts you wrote down.
 Ask what your state does about replacing stolen benefits, because federal replacement ended for thefts on or after 21 December 2024 and the rule now depends on the state.
 5 Step 5 : Report it and block the sender
 Report the text or call to your state's attorney general or consumer protection office. Then delete the message and block the number on your iPhone or Android phone.
 A blocked number does not stop new scam texts from other numbers, so keep the rule: nobody who texts you gets the PIN.
 6 Step 6 : Ignore offers to get the money back
 Someone who calls or writes to offer help recovering stolen benefits for a fee is part of the same kind of fraud. Official help with SNAP is free. Your SNAP office and your state's EBT line are the only places to ask.
 Questions about EBT scam
 Is the EBT text that says my card is locked real?
 Treat it as a scam. USDA's SNAP scam alerts say criminals send fake texts claiming that a SNAP EBT card is locked, and the text includes a phone number to call. USDA's advice is not to give your EBT card number or PIN by phone or text.
 To be sure about your card, find the customer service number on the back of the card yourself and call that, or contact your local SNAP office. If the card has a real problem, they can tell you without asking for your PIN in a message.
 What is the EBT scam?
 It is a group of tricks aimed at EBT cards, not one single scheme. The common ones are fake texts and calls that ask for the card number and PIN, skimmers placed on store card readers that copy the magnetic stripe, and fake offers or fake help that ask for details or a fee.
 The FTC and USDA describe the first two, and state consumer alerts describe the third. All of them end the same way: thieves use a copy of the card or the PIN to spend the balance.
 What should I do if I gave my EBT PIN to a scammer?
 Change it the same day. Call the customer service number on the back of your card, which you found on the card and not in a message, and ask to change the PIN or cancel and replace the card.
 Then check the balance and transactions for charges you did not make, and tell your local SNAP office, as USDA advises when benefits are stolen. Report the scam to your state's attorney general or consumer protection office, and keep the text or the call details for the report.
 Will I get my stolen EBT benefits back?
 Not always. News coverage of the USDA notice says benefits stolen on or after 21 December 2024 cannot be replaced with federal funds, and that states may choose to replace them with state money without any guarantee.
 Thefts from 1 October 2022 to 20 December 2024 could still be claimed through state agencies. We could not confirm each state's rule today. Report the theft fast and ask your local SNAP office what your state does now, because the answer depends on your state.
 How does EBT card skimming work?
 A criminal fits an illegal skimmer onto a payment terminal in a store. The skimmer reads the magnetic stripe when you swipe. Since an EBT card needs a PIN, the thieves either watch for it with a hidden camera near the reader or phish it by text or call, as the FTC alert of May 2024 describes.
 They then make a duplicate card and drain the benefits. Chip cards are harder to copy, and USDA has recommended that states move to them.
 Does a real benefits office ever text me?
 Offices can send reminders in some places, but none of them asks for your card number or PIN by text or phone. The New Jersey consumer alert we read says state agencies and SNAP workers will never ask for such details over the phone or by text.
 It also says that no agency contacts recipients unsolicited for private information and that help getting SNAP benefits is always free. If a message asks for the PIN, it is a scam whatever it says about who sent it.
 Who can I report an EBT scam to?
 Start with your local SNAP office if benefits were taken, and your state's attorney general or consumer protection office for the message or call. 
 In New Hampshire, the attorney general's notice from November 2025 lists 1-844-ASK-DHHS for the benefits agency and 1-888-468-4454 for the Consumer Protection Bureau; those numbers are for that state only. In other states, look up your own state's offices on its official website and type the address yourself.
 Is an EBT generator, free EBT or EBT bonus offer real?
 No source we read supports any such offer, and we found nothing that describes a working EBT generator. Benefits are given by your state after you apply, and help is free.
 An offer of extra benefits, a bonus or an EBT balance for a fee is a hook for your card details, your personal data or your money. Do not enter anything and do not pay. This is our reading from the warnings we read, not a test of any named page.
 Is it safe to check my EBT balance on my phone?
 Yes, if you use your state's official EBT site or app, reached by an address you type yourself or a link on a letter from your state, or if you call the number on the back of the card. 
 The danger is the link in a text. Do not tap that, even when it looks official. We could not test any state's app for this page, so use the address your state gives on its own website and check the balance often.
